sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Seirḗn** (*seiren*) — The Song on the Rocks — belongs to the Greek tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Enchanting Singer". The name means "Binder, entangler"[^1].

Seirḗn is the most intelligent monster in the Odyssey: she does not promise pleasure but knowledge — "we know everything that happens on the fruitful earth." The Greeks feared her because her offer is exactly what the wise cannot refuse.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Seirḗn** and serves its temple at [seirḗn.com](https://xn--seirn-yd1b.com). The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *seiren* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Greek as **Σειρήν**. Etymologically it means "Binder, entangler"[^1].

The ASCII form *seiren* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Seirḗn** recovers both the stress accent and the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The original carries both stress and vowel length, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **s** → **S** — S uppercase
- **e** → **e** — e same
- **i** → **i** — i same
- **r** → **r** — r same
- **e** → **ḗ** — Stress + length
- **n** → **n** — n same

The project holds the domain **seirḗn.com** (xn--seirn-yd1b.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Odyssey.
Apollonius Rhodius.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/sɛː.rɛ̌ːn/** — Attic Greek.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: say-RAIN, stacked macron+acute on the final ē.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Greek** — Σειρήν
- **Latin** — Siren
- **French** — sirène
- **Owned form** — Seirḗn

Greek Σειρήν carries the accent on the final syllable — Seirḗn — and the etymology is contested: folk tradition heard σεῖρα, "cord," for the binding song, while modern scholarship looks to Semitic or pre-Greek roots. The macron on the eta preserves the long vowel of the nominative.

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Seirḗn is the most intelligent monster in the Odyssey: she does not promise pleasure but knowledge — "we know everything that happens on the fruitful earth." The Greeks feared her because her offer is exactly what the wise cannot refuse.[^1]

### The Song

Not seduction but information: the Sirens sing the Trojan War to the man who fought it.

### The Mast

Odysseus bound, crew deafened with wax — the original architecture of resisting temptation.

### Orpheus' Counter-Song

The Argonauts were saved not by wax but by art: Orpheus out-sang the Sirens themselves.

### Bird and Maiden

The Greek form — woman's head on a bird's body; the fishtail mermaid is a medieval graft.

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Seirḗn concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The lyre** — Song as the instrument of capture — art's dangerous edge
- **The meadow of bones** — The flowering shore ringed with the rotting skins of the enchanted
- **The wax** — Deliberate deafness — the technology of the will

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Daughters of the river-god Achelōos and a Muse — Melpomenē or Terpsichorē in the later accounts — the Seirḗnes unite the authority of water and the authority of song.[^1]

### Odyssey 12 (The Passage)

Kirkē warns Odysseus: the Sirens "enchant all who come near," and their island is heaped with bones. He has his crew plug their ears with wax and lash him to the mast. The Sirens hail him by name — they know his story — and promise that whoever hears them sails away "wiser." He strains at the ropes; the ship passes; the danger is measured in the distance of a song.[^2]

### Out-Sung by Orpheus (The Contest)

Apollonius Rhodius sends the Argonauts past the same shore: one crewman, Boutēs, leaps overboard in surrender, but Orpheus strikes his lyre and drowns the enchantment in a nobler song. Later tradition completes the logic — defeated by Odysseus or Orpheus, the Sirens throw themselves into the sea and become rocks: a song that fails to bind has no reason to exist.

### The Lost Wings (The Plaint)

In Euripides' Helen and later lyric, the Sirens are mourners: they searched the world for the abducted Persephonē and were given — or kept — their wings for the search. It is the myth behind the monster: grief transformed into inquiry, the song that asks after the lost girl forever.

### Companions of Persephonē (The Maidens)

The fullest genealogy makes them the girlhood companions of Persephonē: they were playing with her in the meadow when Hádēs struck, and they asked the gods for wings to search the world for her. In Ovid's telling their transformation is their answer to failure — half bird, half maiden forever, still calling across the sea for the lost girl. The myth explains everything about them: the song that stops ships is a search that never ended, and the sailors it kills are drowned in someone else's grief.

sources.citation: Apollonius Rhodius, Argonautica, Loeb Classical Library, 200 BCE.
Euripides, Tragedies, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 406 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Late antiquity moralized her: Christian writers made the Sirens the seductions of the world, the mast the cross. The Middle Ages merged her with the fish-tailed northern mermaid — the bird-maiden of Greece becoming the siren of romance — and French gave the world sirène, which is why modern alarm sirens and mermaids share a word. Kafka's parable "The Silence of the Sirens" gave her the last modern turn: a more fatal weapon than song is silence.[^1]

Within the Greek tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[acheron|Achérōn]], [[achilleus|Achilleús]], [[adamas|Adámas]], [[aer|Aḗr]], [[aither|Aithḗr]], and [[ananke|Anánkē]].

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: "Siren song" is the fixed phrase for an irresistible, ruinous offer; "siren" became the alarm that itself enchants. Adorno and Horkheimer made Odysseus-at-the-mast the parable of the bourgeois self — pleasure permitted only under bondage — and feminist readings recover the Sirens as the suppressed voice of female knowledge. Ambulance sirens, film mermaids, and every warning that allures are her descendants.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: Greek art fixes her form early: bird-bodied, woman-headed, from the 7th century BCE — the famous Attic black-figure stamnos in the British Museum shows Odysseus bound to the mast beneath two enormous birds with women's faces. South Italian funerary art made Sirens the musicians of the dead, carved on tombs of Campania and Apulia as mourning escorts. Odyssey-related localizations — the Sirenum scopuli off the Amalfi coast — are ancient tourism, reported already by Strabo.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

sections.label: Homeric Hymns
sections.body: The corpus contains no hymn to the Seirḗnes — fittingly: their own song is the only one they have. Their hymnic presence is the Odyssey's, which reports the song's opening lines ("Come here, renowned Odysseus, great glory of the Achaeans") and so preserves antiquity's most quoted specimen of enchantment. Later tradition gives them parents from the hymnic world — a Muse for a mother — and Euripides' *Helen* (167–178) gives them their one tragic aria, the invocation to the winged maidens to join her lament. It is the closest Greek tragedy comes to letting them sing on stage.

sources.citation: Homer, Odyssey 12.184–191; Euripides, Helen 167–178.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
The lyric and dramatic tradition names the Sirens by their voices.

- **λιγύριαι (ligýriai)** — 'clear-toned'; the standing Homeric epithet of their song.
- **Θελξιέπεια (Thelxépeia)** — 'Soothing-Words'; one of the three Sirens named in later lists.
- **Μολπή (Molpḗ)** — 'Song'; another of the named three — the art itself as a name.
- **Ἀχελῳάδες (Akhelōiádes)** — 'daughters of Achelōos'; the river-lineage that ties them to water.
- **Μουσικαί** — 'the musical ones'; the title their Muse-mother gives them in the Argonaut tradition.

sources.citation: Apollodorus, Epitome 7.18; Euripides, Helen 167–178.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: The Sirens' geography is the Odyssey's mapped onto real water: the **Sirenusae** — the Li Galli islets off the Sorrentine peninsula — were pointed out to Roman travelers as their meadow, and Strabo records the local traditions of a temple of Athēnā on the cape founded by Odysseus himself. Their true sanctuaries, however, were tombs: in South Italy, Sirens were carved on funerary monuments as musicians of the dead — the bird-maidens who sing the soul across the other, greater sea. The British Museum's famous Odysseus stamnos and the Paestum tomb-paintings preserve this cult face of the enchantresses.

sources.citation: Strabo 5.4.8; on funerary Sirens, see the South Italian tomb corpora.

sections.label: Iconography
sections.body: The early image is exact: a bird's body, a woman's head — never a fish-tail. The **British Museum stamnos** (ca. 475 BCE) shows Odysseus bound to the mast beneath two enormous bird-maidens; a third plunges headlong into the sea, the suicide of the defeated song. South Italian funerary art adopted them as mourning musicians of the tomb (Paestum paintings, Campanian reliefs), sirens with lyres flanking the deceased. The mermaid form is medieval, when the northern fish-tailed siren absorbed the Greek bird-maiden — an iconographic annexation that the alarm-word "sirène" still commemorates.

sources.citation: British Museum 1843,1103.31 (Odysseus stamnos); LIMC VIII.1, s.v. Seirenes.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Seirḗn is the patroness of dangerous knowledge — the truth that costs the listener his course. The Greeks' answer was not ignorance but engineering: hear the song, keep the ropes. Her question remains the sharpest in the Odyssey: if a voice offered to tell you everything, could you sail past it?

Her question has only sharpened in the age of the infinite song. Every feed is the meadow now — a voice that knows your name, your war, your wants, and promises wisdom if you only stop rowing. The Odyssey's answer was never ignorance: hear everything, keep the ropes, and let your crew row deaf through the meadow of bones. Attention is the last navigable strait, and she still sings on both shores of it.

Notice what the myth never does: it never silences them. The Greeks kept the song on their vases, their tombs, their stages — the danger preserved in full voice, ropes and all. That is the tradition's real instruction: do not destroy the enchantment, bind yourself honestly to your course, and let the singing continue. Some knowledge is only safe underway.[^1]
